name: Who Profits: Cost Curve Kings
deck: When commodity prices spike, they no longer compress the earnings of integrated giants. Instead, large operators with hedging power and low breakeven costs pass the shock downstream to smaller buyers and consumers who cannot hedge. The cost curve kings—producers with unit costs far below commodity spot prices—capture the upside while everyone else absorbs the risk.
core_bet: The modern commodity system is no longer a unified cost absorption. Large producers with pricing power and financial infrastructure have engineered pass-through contracts and contract structures that systematically shift commodity risk away from themselves and onto the next layer—smaller operators, converters, consumers. When nitrogen prices surge or cocoa costs spike, the burden lands on farmers, packagers, construction buyers, and households.

mechanism: Large integrated commodity producers—CF Industries, Glencore, Freeport-McMoRan, ConocoPhillips—have hedging infrastructure, financial depth, and global sourcing flexibility. When commodity prices rise, they either have locked in supply at lower costs or can quickly activate hedges. They then negotiate pass-through clauses with customers one tier down: packagers like Crown Holdings and Mondelez, or downstream converters like Cleveland-Cliffs. The key mechanism is the pass-through lag and the pricing power asymmetry. Fixed-price contracts amplify the whiplash for smaller operators. Cleveland-Cliffs locks 35-40% of flat-rolled steel sales under fixed annual automotive contracts. When material costs spike, the company absorbs the margin hit for the contract term. When prices fall, the automaker holds the contract price fixed and captures the benefit.
why_now: Post-2022 commodity volatility never fully settled. Geopolitical disruptions remain endemic: Iran-related fertilizer supply fragility, Middle East energy conflicts, DRC cobalt production quotas, Indonesian mining regulations. CF Industries explicitly described tight global nitrogen supply and the way Iran-related disruption exposed how fragile the nitrogen chain remains. Glencore's CEO linked marketing profits directly to Middle East conflict benefits. These are not one-time shocks; they are structural supply scarcities that keep getting extended. Simultaneously, companies have had two years to harden their pass-through contract infrastructure and pricing power differentials. The transfer mechanism is now institutionalized.
who_pays: Farmers buying nitrogen fertilizer. When CF Industries earnings surge on tight nitrogen markets, farmers absorb higher fertilizer costs and adjust acreage or yields downward. Consumers buying packaged treats and beverages. When Mondelez faces unprecedented cocoa cost headwinds, it passes price increases downstream; consumers see higher Oreo and Cadbury prices and buy fewer units. Construction contractors and automotive makers buying finished steel. When Cleveland-Cliffs' materials costs rise faster than fixed contracts allow, the company absorbs the loss. Small businesses and converters without hedging infrastructure absorb price shocks directly.
who_profits: Integrated commodity producers with low breakeven costs and hedging infrastructure: CF Industries (nitrogen), ConocoPhillips (oil and gas), Suncor (oil sands), Freeport-McMoRan (copper—unit costs $1.97/lb while realized prices $6.17/lb in Q2 2026). Commodity traders with physical assets and marketing arms. Glencore explicitly captures value from supply disruptions and freight volatility through its marketing business. Any operator with pricing power strong enough to pass increases downstream faster than cost inflation arrives.
tension: Consumer affordability breaks the chain. Mondelez showed that when commodity pass-through hits the shelf price, volume declines. Organic net revenue grew only 4.3% in 2025 despite higher selling prices—the growth was anchored by pricing, not volume. At some price point, the consumer cannot absorb more. They trade down, buy fewer units, or switch to cheaper brands. When volume collapses, the entire margin structure inverts. The most vulnerable operators—those without hedging, without long-term contracts, without scale—bear the full volatility in both directions.
surprising_part: The most counterintuitive part is that commodity whiplash is no longer a problem that integrated companies absorb together. Large operators have found ways to systematically shift volatility to smaller operators while protecting their own margins. Cleveland-Cliffs fixed-price contracts are the clearest proof: the company does not just fail to capture upside; it actively absorbs downside in ways its customers avoid. Glencore's marketing business is the structural answer to this trend: if you cannot hide from volatility as a pure producer, become a trader who profits from it.
one_sentence: Commodity price swings no longer hit integrated producers—they are systematically passed downstream to smaller operators, converters, and consumers, concentrating financial risk among those with the least ability to hedge.
societal_stake: The companies with the most sophisticated financial infrastructure bear the least commodity risk. The people with none bear the most. A farmer buying fertilizer, a household buying snacks, a small contractor buying steel—none have the hedging tools, contract power, or scale that CF Industries or Glencore command. When commodity prices shock the system, the cost absorption cascades backward to the least-protected layer. This is a hidden driver of affordability pressure in middle-income households and a persistent squeeze on small and medium-sized industrial operators. The physical and financial infrastructure of modern markets makes this transfer systematic rather than random.

evidence.cf_industries: 2025 net earnings $1.46 billion driven by higher average selling prices; Q1 2026 emphasized tight global nitrogen supply and Iran-related disruption exposing fertilizer supply fragility; farmers absorb the cost while CF captures the upside
evidence.mondelez: 2025 described as 'unprecedented cocoa cost headwinds'; full-year net revenues $38.537B with organic growth of 4.3% but EPS under pressure; consumers face price increases from commodity pass-through
evidence.glencore: H1 2026 Marketing Adjusted EBIT rose to $3.3B, up 142%; CEO explicitly cited Middle East conflict benefits; cobalt production shifted to copper as prices diverged, monetizing supply-chain disruptions
evidence.freeport_mcmoran: Q2 2026 unit net cash costs steady at $1.97 per pound copper while realized prices hit $6.17 per pound; byproduct economics from gold and molybdenum provide cushion; producers at this cost level capture upside while downstream buyers pay more
evidence.cleveland_cliffs: 2025 GAAP net loss $1.4 billion partly driven by persistently weak automotive production and lagging fixed annual contract pricing; 35-40% of flat-rolled sales locked in fixed contracts—the company bears the whiplash auto OEMs avoided
evidence.crown_holdings: Q1 2026 navigated Middle East conflict via global sourcing flexibility; aluminum and steel pass-through contracts protect converter margins while beverage brands face input cost pressure
evidence.eastman_kodak: Q1 2026 higher silver and aluminum prices explicitly offset part of operational gain; Q2 2026 gross profit improved 61% but AM&C revenue growth was constrained by higher commodity inputs
